title: Cantucci di Prato
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Twice-baked Tuscan almond biscuits, hard and crunchy by design, traditionally served alongside a glass of sweet Vin Santo for dunking.
longDesc: The double-bake process — first as a log, then sliced and toasted again — is what gives cantucci their signature crunch and long shelf life, a practical Tuscan tradition that has become one of Italy's most beloved cookies.
ingredients: 3 eggs, plus 1 extra for egg wash
200 g (1½ cups) whole almonds, skin on
steps: Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt in a bowl.
Add the eggs and orange zest, mixing until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms.
Divide the dough in half and shape each portion into a log about 5cm wide on a lined baking sheet.
Brush the logs with beaten egg and bake at 180°C (350°F) for 25 minutes until golden and firm.
Remove from the oven and let cool for 10–15 minutes, just until cool enough to handle.
Using a sharp serrated knife, slice the logs on a diagonal into biscuits about 1.5cm thick.
Lay the slices cut-side down on the baking sheet and bake again for 12–15 minutes, until dry and golden on both sides.
Cool completely — the biscuits will continue to harden as they cool.
chefTips: Let the baked logs cool just slightly before slicing — too hot and they crumble, too cool and they're harder to cut cleanly.
A serrated knife with a firm, decisive cut gives the cleanest slices without crumbling.
These genuinely improve with age, keeping well for weeks in an airtight container.
commonMistakes: Slicing the log while still too hot, causing the biscuits to crumble apart.
Underbaking the second round, leaving the biscuits too soft rather than achieving their signature crunch.
Skimping on the almonds, which are central to the texture and flavor of a proper cantuccio.
servedWith: A glass of Vin Santo, for dunking
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 weeks.
reheating: Not applicable; these are meant to be crunchy and are not reheated.
healthBenefits: Almonds provide healthy fats, protein, and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Cantucci take their alternate name, biscotti di Prato, from the Tuscan city where they originated, and their long shelf life made them a practical staple for travelers for centuries.
